issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the threat profile, which is dominated by fear-based hypervigilance and exaggerated startle. In this profile it introduces a more externalizing response pattern that is not supported elsewhere in memory, appraisals, triggers, or strategies.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: Betrayal by a trusted person does not fit well with the stated trauma type of civilian in a war zone unless there is evidence of an interpersonal betrayal trauma, which is otherwise absent from the profile. The rest of the items center on war exposure, victims, grief, loss of control, and danger rather than trusted-person betrayal.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: Reminders of victims fit war-zone exposure, but paired with perpetrator-focused avoidance and betrayal appraisals they imply a specific interpersonal-harm narrative that is not otherwise coherently represented. The profile oscillates between mass-trauma civilian exposure and a perpetrator-betrayal formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: Avoiding cues related to the person who harmed me implies a discrete perpetrator-centered trauma. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which more strongly reflects civilian war-zone exposure, victims, grief, and generalized threat rather than a single identifiable assailant.

vignette:
Rajan had been painting houses in the same Boston suburb for over twenty years, a trade he had learned from his father after immigrating from Gujarat. His life had been one of quiet, steady rhythms-the smell of fresh paint, the scrape of a brush, the satisfaction of a finished room. That ended on a Tuesday afternoon in September, three years ago, when he had stopped at a market in a busy plaza. A delivery truck backfired, and a split second later, a man near the entrance dropped a heavy metal tray. The sound was a flat, percussive crack that seemed to come from everywhere at once. For Rajan, the world collapsed into a single, frozen moment. He was no longer in the plaza; he was back in the narrow alley behind his uncle's shop in Ahmedabad, pinned against a wall as mortar fire rained down around him. He had been twenty-three, a civilian caught in a crossfire he had spent thirty years trying to forget. In the plaza, he had dropped to his knees, his hands over his ears, his body locked in a tight, protective curl, just as it had been in that alley. When the memory came, it was not a story he told himself; it was a physical reenactment. He felt the grit of the alley wall against his back, the crushing weight of his own body trying to disappear. And with that memory came a wave of grief so profound it stole his breath-grief for the boy he had been, for the uncle who had died that day, for the life of simple meaning he had built since.

In the weeks that followed, the world rearranged itself around that sound. A car door slamming in the street, a child dropping a book in the library, the clatter of a paint can in his own truck-each one could trigger the same visceral plunge. He had come to believe that the world was a fundamentally dangerous place, that safety was an illusion he could no longer afford. The market, the plaza, the busy intersections he had once navigated without thought-these became zones of constant threat. He began to work harder at keeping busy, taking on double shifts, painting through lunch, filling every silent moment with the scrape of a roller or the hum of a radio. What frightened him most was the stillness, because in stillness the memories came. He would find himself in a quiet room, and suddenly his body would lock into that same frozen crouch, his muscles braced for an impact that never came. He was certain he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him-of being the calm, reliable father and husband his family knew. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore; the satisfaction he had once taken in a clean, straight line of paint had evaporated. He had started to avoid the news, switching off the television whenever reports mentioned conflict or violence, because those images fed the loop. He would ruminate for hours, going over and over why the event had happened to him, why he had survived when his uncle had not, as if finding an answer might undo the memory.

The causal connections tightened into a relentless cycle. The triggers-the bang of a door, the crack of a dropped tool-would instantly activate his threat system, leaving him hypervigilant, his body constantly tense and ready to react. His wife noticed he jumped at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people. He was always on guard, scanning rooms for exits, watching people's hands. This state of threat made the memories more accessible; when he was already tense, the flashbacks came more easily, and they brought with them the overwhelming grief. That grief, in turn, reinforced his belief that the world was dangerous and his life meaningless, which made him even more vigilant. His avoidance strategies-the frantic busyness, the refusal to watch the news-were intended to control the triggers, but they had the opposite effect. By never allowing himself to process the event, the memory remained raw and extreme, so hard to believe it had actually happened to him. The more he avoided, the more potent the triggers became. A single smell, like the diesel exhaust from a delivery truck, could send him into a full reenactment, his body locked in that same position, his mind lost in the past. The threat state made him hypervigilant to new triggers, which meant he was constantly scanning for sounds, and those sounds would trigger the memory again. The memory, in turn, fed his negative appraisals, deepening his conviction that he was no longer capable and that the world was a dangerous place. These appraisals made the triggers feel more imminent, more personal, more inevitable.

He had stopped taking jobs in busy commercial areas, telling his boss he preferred residential work. He avoided the plaza entirely. He began to feel his body constantly tense, even at home, even in bed. The cycle had ground down his marriage; his wife felt she was living with a stranger who flinched at her touch. What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a moment in his own kitchen, when his daughter dropped a glass. The shattering sound sent him to the floor, his hands over his head, his breath ragged, and he could not get up for several minutes. He was terrified that he was losing his mind. He was most afraid that he would never feel safe again, but he was also, quietly, hoping that someone might help him find a way to live with the memory without being consumed by it.
